name: The Meselson-Stahl Experiment
aliases: The most beautiful experiment in biology
statement: By weighing DNA made with heavy then light nitrogen, the experiment showed each new helix keeps one old strand.
statementAccent: each new helix keeps one old strand
meaning: The Meselson-Stahl experiment was a molecular-biology experiment carried out by Matthew Meselson and Franklin Stahl at Caltech in 1957 and 1958, which determined how DNA copies itself, confirming that DNA replication is semiconservative. After Watson and Crick proposed the double-helix structure of DNA in 1953, three ways it might replicate were considered: semiconservative, in which each new double helix keeps one of the two original strands and pairs it with a newly made strand; conservative, in which the original helix stays fully intact and an entirely new helix is built alongside it; and dispersive, in which the strands are broken up and old and new pieces are interspersed. To distinguish these, Meselson and Stahl grew bacteria for many generations in a medium containing a heavy isotope of nitrogen so that all their DNA was heavy, then switched them to normal light nitrogen and sampled the DNA after successive generations, separating the molecules by their density. After one generation all the DNA was of intermediate weight, and after two generations half was intermediate and half was light, exactly the pattern predicted by semiconservative replication. The result confirmed the semiconservative model and is often called the most beautiful experiment in biology.
mechanism: The experiment worked by making DNA distinguishable by weight and watching how that weight was inherited as the DNA replicated. Meselson and Stahl grew the bacterium Escherichia coli for many generations in a medium whose only nitrogen was the heavy isotope nitrogen-15, so that all the nitrogen-containing bases of the bacteria's DNA were heavy and the DNA had a high density. They then abruptly transferred the bacteria to a medium containing only ordinary light nitrogen-14, so that any DNA strands made from then on would be light, and they took samples of the population after each round of replication. To measure the density of the DNA, they used cesium chloride density-gradient centrifugation, spinning the DNA at high speed in a salt solution until each molecule settled at the level matching its density, forming a visible band. Before the switch, the DNA formed a single heavy band. After exactly one generation in light nitrogen, all the DNA formed a single band of intermediate density, meaning every molecule was half heavy and half light, which is only possible if each new helix has one old heavy strand and one new light strand. After two generations, the DNA split into two bands, half intermediate and half fully light. This pattern matched semiconservative replication and ruled out the conservative model, which would have shown separate heavy and light bands from the first generation, and the dispersive model.

examples.text: Bacteria grown in heavy nitrogen-15 were switched to light nitrogen-14 so newly made DNA strands would be lighter and distinguishable.
After one generation all the DNA was of intermediate density, each helix half old and half new, as semiconservative replication predicts.
A single intermediate band, not separate heavy and light bands, ruled out conservative replication, and the later pattern ruled out dispersive.

variants.name: The three models
variants.text: The semiconservative, conservative, and dispersive hypotheses for DNA replication that the experiment set out to distinguish.

variants.name: Density-gradient centrifugation
variants.text: The technique of separating DNA molecules by their density in a cesium chloride gradient, which made the weights visible as bands.

whyItMatters: The Meselson-Stahl experiment is one of the most elegant and important experiments in the history of biology, because it revealed the fundamental mechanism by which genetic information is copied and passed on. When Watson and Crick proposed the double helix in 1953, they suggested that the two strands might separate and each serve as a template for a new partner, but this was only a hypothesis; Meselson and Stahl proved it, showing conclusively that DNA replicates semiconservatively, with each daughter molecule keeping one original strand. This confirmed the deep logic of the double helix, explaining how DNA can be faithfully duplicated so that genetic information is preserved from one generation of cells to the next, and it became a foundation of molecular genetics. The experiment is also celebrated as a model of experimental design, so clean and decisive that it was famously dubbed the most beautiful experiment in biology, a phrase associated with the biologist John Cairns. Its density-gradient method became a widely used tool.

working.text: grow bacteria for many generations in heavy nitrogen so all their DNA is dense.
transfer the bacteria to light nitrogen and sample the DNA after successive rounds of replication.
separate the DNA by density and find one intermediate band after one generation, confirming each helix keeps an old strand.

limits: The Meselson-Stahl experiment is remarkably clean, but a few points deserve care. The bench work ran from 1957 into 1958 and was published in 1958, so it is best dated to 1957 to 1958 rather than a single year. It demonstrated the semiconservative mechanism in the bacterium E. coli, and although semiconservative replication is now known to be universal, that generality rested on further work extending the result to other organisms. The experiment showed the overall pattern of strand inheritance but not the detailed molecular machinery of replication, the enzymes and steps of copying, which were worked out separately. The famous description of it as the most beautiful experiment in biology is an evaluative phrase associated with John Cairns and popularized later, not a claim by Meselson or Stahl.
misreadings: The Meselson-Stahl experiment did not reveal the full machinery of DNA replication; it showed the pattern, that each new helix keeps one old strand, not the enzymes and steps that carry copying out. It demonstrated this in bacteria, so its universality rested on further work, though semiconservative replication is now known to be general. And the label most beautiful experiment in biology is a later evaluation, not the experimenters' own claim, so treating the experiment as explaining the whole replication process, as immediately universal, or as self-proclaimed beautiful, misreads a decisive demonstration of semiconservative replication.
origin: A molecular-biology experiment by Matthew Meselson and Franklin Stahl at Caltech in 1957 to 1958, using heavy and light nitrogen and density-gradient centrifugation to confirm that DNA replicates semiconservatively.
